vectors.enisa_quote: disrupt communications between the ground station and the satellite, or vice versa
vectors.reason: A jammer is external RF equipment acting on the TT&C space-ground link ENISA names.

vectors.enisa_quote: disrupt communications between the ground station and the satellite
vectors.reason: ENISA's ground station is the TTC station, but a gateway is also a ground station and the feeder link is a ground-satellite link; the text only implies it.
ENISA lists 'User: VSAT' among the targets and says 'space-link communication'; a jammer or rogue terminal on the service link is implied, not stated.

rows.sparta_quote: any actor-controlled transmitter, platform, or node
rows.reason: The jammer is an outside transmitter on the link; SPARTA notes such entities may apply interference rather than mission-compatible signals.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: Sending the unauthorized guidance and control commands ENISA lists as a jamming result needs a mission-compatible transmitter that overpowers the legitimate signal.

rows.enisa_quote: Overpowering the frequency of a legitimate RF signal
rows.sparta_quote: electronic attack that uses radio frequency energy to deny the use of a signal
rows.reason: This is the overpowering of a legitimate RF signal that ENISA defines as jamming.

rows.enisa_quote: disrupt communications between the ground station and the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: Uplink jamming prevents acceptance of telecommands
rows.reason: The ground-to-satellite direction of the disrupted link is uplink jamming of the telecommand channel, which only a transmitter on the TT&C link can do.

rows.sparta_quote: Downlink jammers target the users of a satellite
rows.reason: The satellite-to-ground direction ('or vice versa') is downlink jamming, which also reaches VSAT users.

rows.sparta_quote: overwhelm/jam the downlink signal to prevent transmitted telemetry signals from reaching their destination
rows.reason: Jamming the satellite-to-ground telemetry downlink is the 'or vice versa' direction; SPARTA files it under Defense Evasion but the act is the same jamming, aimed at the ground controller's receiver on the TT&C link.

rows.enisa_quote: Jamming can result in unauthorized commands for guidance and control being sent to the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may inject an unauthorized command or alter a legitimate command before execution
rows.reason: ENISA states unauthorized commands reaching the satellite as a result; IA-0008.01 is the step that sends them.

rows.sparta_quote: An adversary may modify executable code, replace firmware, or load altered programmable logic
rows.reason: ENISA states injection of malicious code as a result; the code reaches the satellite through the same command channel IA-0008.01 opens, so no separate loading step is kept (loading is TR46).

rows.sparta_quote: The resource may support computing, storage, or communications.
rows.reason: ENISA states denial of service; the contested resource is the communications channel, a link-only outcome.
The parent also covers crashing telemetry software and falsified telemetry content; ENISA jamming matches only the jam variant DE-0002.02, which is kept.
ENISA jamming acts on the link, not on ground telemetry processing.
ENISA jamming does not suppress telemetry at the source on board.

Replay of command packets is not described.

Defeating encryption is TR45 (cryptographic exploit), which keeps it; ENISA jamming mentions no crypto attack.
ENISA jamming does not involve inducing bit flips.

Flooding with valid commands is TR40 (DoS), which keeps it; not the jamming ENISA describes.

GNSS-band jamming is not what ENISA describes: the text names the ground-satellite communication link, and the guidance and control commands it mentions are not a navigation-signal effect.

Proximity exfiltration is not described and no kept row needs it.
Reconfiguring communications to leak data is not described.
Tampering at manufacture or delivery is TR55 (supply-chain compromise), which keeps it; jamming is an RF act during operation.
Poisoned dependencies and build tools are TR55, which keeps it; not jamming.

Altered hardware before delivery is TR55, which keeps it; not jamming.
Compromising a software-defined radio is not described.
No crosslink path is described.
Forcing the satellite onto a backup channel by jamming is not described by ENISA.
Using a backup or standby ground station; ENISA jamming names no backup path.
Jamming the primary to open the backup receiver is not described by ENISA.
Proximity operations are not described; ENISA gives no spacecraft-based jammer.
Emanation analysis is not described.
Riding a docking or servicing event; ENISA jamming names no co-orbital or physical actor.
Grappling the satellite for physical contact; ENISA jamming names no co-orbital or physical actor.

Compromising the mission ground system; ENISA jamming names no compromised ground system.

ENISA names no change to settings or limits.
ENISA names no falsified or corrupted data.
ENISA names no timing or synchronization change.
Pivoting from a hosted payload across the host-payload boundary; ENISA jamming names no hosted payload.

ENISA does not say the commands rely on prior study of the command scheme.

IMP-0012 still has no dedicated action: kept because ENISA states 'injection of malicious code' as a result.
